source.title: From superposition to sparse codes: interpretable representations in neural networks
source.authors: David A. Klindt; Charles O'Neill; P. Reizinger; Harald Maurer; N. Miolane

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses representation theory and reports an additivity example, but does not test whether representations converge across models, modalities, seeds, or scale. Cross-model convergence results mentioned in the text are from cited work.
record.gate_note: The paper's Fig. 1 reports an additivity analysis for image representations, which is relevant to superposition but does not measure any listed claim version. The cited reports of sparse codes converging across networks and other prior findings are not this study's results and are excluded.
record.test_reason: Perspective paper on superposition, identifiability and sparse coding. Its only empirical results are an additivity test on ViT-B/16 (Fig. 1) and an analogy example (Fig. 3, c.s.=0.92) within a single model. None compares representations across models, seeds, modalities or scale. Statements about cross-model convergence of sparse codes (Lan et al., Chen and Bonner) and SAE non-universality (Paulo and Belrose) are cited, not tested. It mentions the Platonic hypothesis only in passing.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance. The authors argue that identifiability theory implies representations are linear in the latent variables, and that sparse coding (via compressed sensing) can recover interpretable features from superposition. They add that quantitative interpretability metrics are needed, and note that SAEs recover features suboptimally. They cite prior work that sparse codes converge across networks, but do not test this.
record.recipe_differences: The paper presents a perspective and an additivity example, not a cross-model convergence measurement or a reproduction of the original sources' methods.

fits_no_version.finding: Within ViT-B/16, the representation of a combined image is close to the sum of its parts' representations. This is significant over a calibrated baseline (p<10^-5) but not in pixel space (p≈0.88).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Image-model representations are approximately additive (linear superposition) over object concepts, unlike pixel space.

fits_no_version.finding: An analogy example in ViT-B/16: elephant + pink ball − ball gives c.s.=0.92 with the pink elephant image (Fig. 3C).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear concept arithmetic holds locally in vision-model representation space.

record.problems: The additivity evidence is limited to the reported image examples; the paper gives no numerical cosine-similarity values, and the N=10 further examples are not shown. It does not assess cross-model convergence or model capability.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Results attributed to cited studies, including claims about cross-network sparse-code convergence, were not extracted as findings of this paper.

untested.parts: No cross-model alignment measured as a function of scale, architecture, objective or data.
No vision–language alignment on paired data.
No stitching, mapping or relative-representation experiments between models.
Universality of SAE features across models is discussed only through cited work, with no new result.
No test of metric or input dependence of convergence.
No measurement of incomplete alignment or of its causes.

missing.what: Analogy-making cosine similarity of 0.92 in ViT-B/16 (Fig. 3C). It is within-model and not on any version, but no row records it.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is not an original source. It invokes cross-model sparse-code convergence as cited support for its framework. It also offers a speculative explanation, suboptimal SAE inference, for why extracted features are not always universal across models (citing Paulo and Belrose). Both are discussion only.

versions.untested_parts: Alignment between independently trained models as a function of scale, capability, architecture, objective, or data.
Cross-modal alignment of paired image and caption representations as model quality changes.
Feature or subspace convergence across random seeds.
Mapping or stitching representations between models, including linear maps, relative representations, or unpaired mappings.
Recurrence of interpretable features or circuits across different models.
Dependence of cross-model convergence on similarity metrics, settings, or input distributions.
Whether cross-model alignment is incomplete or explained by shared data or objectives.
